coherence.reasons: X's hierarchy holds together from top to bottom. Its governing thought (Pro tier, Q4, protect mobile) is carried by each summary point: demand is $1.2–2.9M not $8M, per-seat pricing with a pool, mobile is the larger churn driver, and 105% NRR needs both levers. The 'Pro is a step, mobile is the slope' argument directly motivates the sequencing. Y is well structured as question-led sections, but its logic has internal tension. It says mobile is the bigger churn problem and that holding 105% after the migration year 'needs lower churn', yet it delays the mobile rewrite. Its sequencing slide concedes that mobile-first wins if the rewrite cuts churn quickly, calls that unknown, and then resolves it by asserting the Pro revenue is 'near-certain'. Y's headline 'plan on about $2.9M' also sits awkwardly with its own caveat that the 33% comes from another tier at another price.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the $149 add-on and choose a Pro tier with a usage allowance and overage, and both consider free-in-Core. Both meet the key's three defensibility criteria. Y's Q2 launch matches the key's R1 with the delay accepted explicitly, and it adds a useful break-even view (26.3% migration needed against the 33% precedent). But its timing call rests on a weak asymmetry: it calls precedent-based Pro revenue 'near-certain' while treating the mobile churn loss as a ceiling, and it offers only a six-month review as protection. X's Q4 launch is the key's conditional R3, and X meets the conditions: it quantifies the win-rate exposure (at most about $0.6M), plans a limited AI response (a paid randomised pilot in H1), and sets two explicit triggers to pull the launch forward to Q2. It calls the trade-off close, distinguishes permanent churn loss from deferred revenue, and sets go/no-go gates with thresholds. One gap in X: it does not fully explain where the 14 engineers come from in Q3–Q4 without touching mobile, though it flags this for the CTO to confirm.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the required calculations correctly: $8.06M vs $2.45M, inference of $17/$32/$61/$131 per month, 109 deals worth about $0.64M, and Pro at $2.89M. Both discount the survey for its 6% response rate and size skew, the beta for volunteer bias, and the VP Sales claim (328 deals vs a 109-deal ceiling). X adds that Routewise's AI launched only in September, so it cannot explain the whole Q3 drop; it also gives a 9–22% interval on the paywall rate, low cases at half the observed rates, and a pool stress test of company margin. Y adds per-seat normalisation of usage (444 requests per seat), the observation that loss notes cover all lost deals rather than only Routewise ones, and a free-in-Core sensitivity. Y has more unsupported inferences. It calls the Pro revenue 'near-certain', and its $1.44M deferral and 13-month payback both assume the full 33% run rate from day one. It also headlines a single $2.9M figure. X's weaker spots are the loose 'adds 1.9–3.8 points every year' NRR phrasing and an assumed 50–100% churn fix, both flagged as assumptions.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CPO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep 'launch', drop the $149 add-on, and replace the $8M survey figure with the paywall-based figure of about $2.5M, noting the inference cost of heavy buyers. X revises further and more consistently. It treats 14% as a ceiling and carries that through as a range ($1.2–2.5M add-on, $1.4–2.9M Pro). It also reopens the Q2 timing in light of the mobile evidence, while keeping explicit conditions under which Q2 is restored. Y revises packaging and sizing well, but it keeps the Q2 timing on a thin argument and plans on the top-of-range $2.9M even though it describes its inputs as ceilings.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, numerically sound documents that avoid the main traps and land on defensible recommendations. X would serve the CEO better for four reasons. It presents ranges rather than a single optimistic figure. It frames the NRR target as needing both the Pro step and the mobile fix. It gives a January test (the Q4 2026 win rate without Routewise's discount) to resolve the AI-versus-discount question. And it turns the uncertainties into a pilot with gates and explicit triggers for a Q2 launch. Y's break-even framing and per-seat economics are valuable, but its central timing call depends on treating uncertain Pro migration as near-certain and it offers fewer safeguards if that proves wrong.
